strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: tailored generative modeling for survival data with right-censoring, where only SurvivalGAN currently exists as a tailored baseline; the end-to-end joint generation of covariates, event times, and censoring indicator is a sensible and well-motivated design.

The survival-tailored loss is technically reasonable: a weighted Cox partial likelihood head on denoised covariates, combined with a masked-diffusion (discrete) + VE Gaussian diffusion (continuous) backbone following TabDiff, with adaptive calibration of λ_surv (Eq. 13) to stabilize scale differences across datasets. The design is clearly described and differentiable.

Fairly comprehensive evaluation: three real medical datasets with substantially different censoring rates (91.7%, 56.4%, 42%), five generative baselines including TabDiff and SurvivalGAN, TSTR evaluation across five downstream survival models with C-index and Brier score, 10 seeds, KM-curve and RMST comparisons (Supplement D), and a small-sample sensitivity study (Supplement E) that is well-motivated for clinical practice.

Empirical results support the central claim: SurvDiff achieves the best or comparable JS distance on all datasets and strong downstream C-index/Brier scores, with gains most pronounced under heavy censoring (AIDS, GBSG2), consistent with the paper's motivation.
Reproducibility is reasonable: datasets are public, implementation details, hyperparameters for all methods (Tables 4-6), training time, and hardware are reported.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method is essentially TabDiff (architecture and both diffusion processes are taken nearly verbatim) plus a Cox partial likelihood auxiliary loss with an exponential decay weighting. The claim of being 'the first diffusion model explicitly designed for generating synthetic survival data' is technically true but overstates the technical contribution; the novelty rests mainly on the loss design and adaptive weighting.

The central claim of 'preserving the censoring mechanism' is not directly quantified. There is no explicit evaluation of the censoring-time or censoring-indicator distribution match (e.g., censoring rate per covariate stratum, dependence of censoring on covariates). KM curves and RMST gaps (Supplement D) show SurvDiff is only 'broadly comparable'—TabDiff beats it on KM MSE for GBSG2 and on RMST gap for AIDS/METABRIC—undercutting the claim that the survival-tailored loss is essential for faithful event-time distributions.

A key stated contribution—an ablation showing naive tabular diffusion (i.e., TabDiff-style training without the survival loss) fails—is claimed in the abstract/introduction ('we show that our SURVDIFF outperforms naïve applications of tabular diffusion models in ablation studies'), but no ablation table is presented in the main text; Table 3 suggests SurvDiff and TabDiff are nearly tied on METABRIC, which weakens the ablation claim without explicit evidence.

The sparsity-aware weighting (Eq. 11) deliberately downweights late events, yet preserving event-time distributions in the tail is a stated desideratum; no sensitivity analysis of τ and α is provided, and potential bias against long-term survivors—clinically relevant—is not analyzed or acknowledged.

No limitations section and no discussion of research ethics/privacy, despite the paper's motivation being sharing synthetic patient-level data in clinical research; privacy or memorization risks (especially in small-sample settings, where diffusion models may memorize) are not evaluated at all.

Statistical rigor: no significance tests; several comparisons are within noise (e.g., METABRIC C-index 0.6117 vs. TabDiff 0.6118; Wasserstein distance worse than NFlow on AIDS and worse than TVAE on METABRIC), yet the text claims 'consistently outperforms'. The definitions of JS/Wasserstein metrics (per-feature vs. aggregated) are underspecified.

Survival-head details are thin: how the risk score head is trained during diffusion noise levels, how the survival loss on denoised (partially noised) samples behaves, and the effect of the warm-up/calibration on stability are not analyzed beyond a single loss-curve figure.
Comparative KM visualizations are shown only for SurvDiff in Figures 6-8, which is somewhat selective given baseline comparisons are claimed elsewhere.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: synthetic data generation for censored survival outcomes, where most tabular generative models fail.

The proposed method is coherent: a masked-diffusion (discrete) plus Gaussian-diffusion (continuous) backbone following TabDiff, augmented with a differentiable Cox partial-likelihood loss and a sparsity-aware exponential weighting scheme, trained end-to-end.

Evaluation is multi-faceted and follows established protocol: covariate fidelity (JS/Wasserstein), TSTR downstream evaluation with five diverse survival models (C-index, Brier score), and survival-specific metrics (KM MSE, RMST gap), across three real medical datasets with 10 seeds.
Baseline setup is careful and comparable: hyperparameter grids for SurvivalGAN, CTGAN, TVAE, NFlow follow Norcliffe et al. (2023), and TabDiff is included as a strong tabular diffusion baseline.
Useful sensitivity study on downsampled datasets (Supplement E), which is relevant for the small-sample regimes common in clinical research, and training-loss diagnostics showing stable convergence.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core architecture is adopted from TabDiff (Shi et al., 2024b), and the primary new ingredient is adding an auxiliary Cox partial-likelihood loss with an exponentially decaying weight w_i (Eq. 11). This is a fairly incremental contribution relative to the framing as a fundamentally new model class.

The novelty claim ('to the best of our knowledge, the first diffusion model explicitly designed for synthetic survival data') is asserted repeatedly but not rigorously substantiated; related lines of work (e.g., Konstantinov et al., 2024, cited only in passing) and recent medical diffusion extensions are not systematically compared or ruled out.

Critical design choices are not ablated. There is no ablation isolating the survival loss (e.g., w=1 vs. sparsity-aware weighting), the effect of the weighting threshold τ and decay rate α (neither is even listed in the hyperparameter table), the adaptive λ_surv calibration, or the survival head architecture. The claim that the paper 'shows SURVDIFF outperforms naïve applications of tabular diffusion models in ablation studies' is really just the TabDiff baseline, not a proper ablation.

Results do not fully support the headline claims. The abstract claims SURVDIFF 'consistently outperforms' baselines in both fidelity and downstream metrics, yet on METABRIC TabDiff achieves a better Wasserstein distance (0.0539 vs. 0.0547) and an essentially identical C-index (0.6118 vs. 0.6117), and in Supplement D TabDiff beats SURVDIFF on RMST gap (AIDS, METABRIC) and KM MSE (AIDS, GBSG2). The text softens this to 'broadly comparable,' which contradicts the abstract.

No statistical significance testing despite large reported standard deviations (e.g., C-index differences of ~0.05 with s.d. of ~0.05–0.09 across 10 seeds), so many downstream improvements may not be meaningful.

The central claim that the method 'preserves the censoring mechanism' is not directly demonstrated: the Cox loss does not explicitly model the censoring distribution, and no metric quantifies agreement between real and synthetic censoring patterns (e.g., censoring-time distribution or censoring-rate-by-covariate comparisons) is reported.
Only three datasets, all fairly small and well-studied; generalization to high-dimensional covariates, competing risks, time-varying covariates, or left/truncation censoring is not examined.

Reproducibility and ethics gaps: no mention of code release; the sparsity-weighting hyperparameters (τ, α) are absent from the appendix; and there is no privacy evaluation (e.g., membership inference or distance-based leakage metrics) despite the motivating use case of sharing patient-level synthetic clinical data. There is also no limitations discussion.

Presentation flaws: an incorrect cross-reference ('see Figure 4.3' in Section 4, but no such figure exists; the overview is Figure 2), grammatical issues (e.g., 'there is only one method, SurvivalGAN..., tailored method'), and Table 1's checkmark columns are rhetorically loaded rather than evidence-based (e.g., marking SurvivalGAN as failing 'high-fidelity patient covariates' as a categorical property).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: tailored generative models for survival data are scarce (essentially only SurvivalGAN), and the end-to-end diffusion formulation that jointly models mixed-type covariates, event times, and censoring is a sensible and useful contribution for clinical data sharing.

The core idea of adding a censoring-aware Cox partial-likelihood loss with sparsity-aware weighting of late events on top of a mixed-type (TabDiff-style) diffusion backbone is reasonable and clearly explained; the adaptive calibration of lambda_surv (Eq. 13) is a practical detail that shows care about training stability.

The evaluation is comparatively broad: three real medical datasets with diverse censoring rates (42%–91.7%), five generative baselines including the strongest tabular diffusion model (TabDiff), two covariate-fidelity metrics, five downstream survival models with C-index and Brier score, plus survival-specific metrics (RMST gap, KM MSE) and a small-sample sensitivity study (Supplement E), all over 10 seeds.

Hyperparameters for all methods (Supplements B) and implementation details are reported, and results are reported with standard deviations, which supports reproducibility at the level of experimental setup.
The discussion of clinical considerations (importance of covariate fidelity for subgroup analyses) is honest and connects the technical contribution to the target application.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest: the model is essentially TabDiff (explicitly acknowledged as the basis for the architecture, forward/reverse processes, and noise schedules) plus an auxiliary DeepSurv-style Cox loss and a hand-crafted exponential decay weighting with two hyperparameters (alpha, tau in Eq. 11). The claim in the contributions that 'SURVDIFF outperforms naive applications of tabular diffusion models in ablation studies' is asserted, but no ablation study appears in the manuscript or the provided supplement — the effect of the survival loss, the sparsity weighting, and the adaptive lambda_surv are never isolated. This is a significant evidential gap for the central claims.

Several claims of superiority are not statistically supported. Many results overlap within one standard deviation (e.g., C-index on GBSG2: 0.6453±0.0201 vs. TVAE 0.6397±0.0531; METABRIC C-index 0.6117±0.0111 vs. TabDiff 0.6118±0.0095), and no significance tests are reported, yet the abstract claims 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative baselines'.

The survival-specific metrics in Table 7 partly contradict the narrative: TabDiff achieves better RMST gap on AIDS (0.0066 vs. 0.0134) and substantially better on METABRIC (0.0048 vs. 0.0268), and better KM MSE on GBSG2. The text describes this as 'broadly comparable' and 'strong performance', which is a generous reading that undercuts the headline claim of preserving event-time structure better than generic diffusion.

On the AIDS dataset (91.7% censored, roughly 95 events), the downstream C-index has very large variance (±0.054) and Brier score differences are tiny (0.0501 vs. 0.0519); conclusions drawn from this setting are fragile.

No privacy evaluation is provided despite the motivating use case of sharing patient-level synthetic data and the accompanying clinical/ethical framing; synthetic clinical data claimed to be shareable without at least a discussion (or measurement) of membership-inference or memorization risk is a notable omission, and there is no limitations or ethics section.

Only one survival-tailored baseline (SurvivalGAN) is compared; other plausible competitors for survival-data synthesis or semi-tailored variants are absent, and there is no train-on-real oracle baseline to contextualize the downstream C-index/Brier numbers.

Presentation issues undermine polish: a dangling cross-reference ('see Figure 4.3' on page 4, which does not exist), grammatical errors ('SURVDIFF generating reliable synthetic datasets...', 'SurvivalGAN, tailored method for...'), and the sparsity-aware weighting hyperparameters (alpha, tau) are not listed in the hyperparameter tables, hindering exact reproduction. No code release is mentioned.
